st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: The source is consistent with the cluster’s conditional treatment of adoption claims: it reports qualitative employee buy-in and enthusiasm for legal technology but provides no performance metrics, customer outcomes or demonstrated generative-AI transformation. Its evidence therefore supports distinguishing positive expectations and personal assessments from validated results.

kp.k: Executives predict an AI inflection point for legal services
kp.d: Reveal CEO Wendell Jisa argues that, over the preceding 12 to 18 months, technology adoption has increasingly become a requirement and technology users have become decision-makers. He predicts legal services will be affected more than any other industry and urges cooperation among competing vendors. These are executive expectations, not measured industry findings.
qs: More and more people have recognized the fact that it's a requirement now.
the individuals who are using the technology are now the decision makers.
I personally believe that the legal industry itself will be impacted more than any other industry in the world.

kp.k: Free access aims to build proficiency before purchase
kp.d: The episode announces Aji's planned September 2025 launch and free access through the end of 2025. Jisa frames the offer as an investment in user learning and eventual commercial adoption: users should become proficient before seeking budget approval. He explicitly acknowledges that the software is imperfect.
qs: its decision to offer it completely free through the end of 2025
When you're not paying for something and you're able to become an expert in it, I think it's very empowering.
None of this software is perfect.
when you do invest in it, when you go to get your budget approvals, this, that, or the other, you're going to know how to use it.

kp.k: Review augmentation is prioritized over replacing reviewers
kp.d: CTO Matthew Brothers-McGrew predicts that AI will move practitioners away from sequential document review toward complex problems, case understanding and client value. Drawing an analogy with computer adoption in the 1980s, he rejects replacement as Aji's present objective, while speculating that the market might be ready for it 20 years later. No employment or productivity study is supplied.
qs: it's going to allow people to focus on more complicated problems or to offer more value to their customers rather than having to focus on, you know, document, know, single document review, going doc to doc, 60 documents an hour.
We were very clear. We do not want aji to replace the reviewer.
Look, I mean 20 years down the road. Maybe the markets ready for that
We want it to truly be your partner.

kp.k: Defensibility relies on established review metrics and workflows
kp.d: Brothers-McGrew describes Aji as using off-the-shelf LLMs within a patent-pending human–technology workflow. He reports industry concerns that generative review is untested and lacks court acceptance, and says Reveal addresses these through F1, recall and precision measurements familiar from classical AI review. This is a proposed defensibility strategy, not evidence of judicial acceptance of Aji or reported performance results.
qs: We use off-shelf LLMs, just like most folks do, but it's really about the workflow.
One is it's not tested. No court has really accepted it.
So we have provided the ability for someone to run F1 scores and recall and precision.

The same thing that they already have proven to the court is around the classic AI models and how they prove the efficacy of those models to the court and how they negotiate with the other side to accept that technology.

kp.k: Calibration combines prompt refinement with human-reviewed document comparisons
kp.d: Brothers-McGrew describes an iterative calibration workflow: the LLM first requests clarification of review instructions, then Reveal's Ask search product selects responsive, non-responsive and intermediate documents. In his illustrative workflow, roughly 100 documents receive human review; AI and human classifications are compared, and disagreements inform suggested prompt changes. These numbers describe a workflow example, not a validation study.
qs: So the LLM is actually evaluating what you're telling it before you look at a single document and telling you what's good and what's bad about the way you're interacting with me.
give me 15 documents or 20 documents that are highly responsive to these issues and find 15 or 20 documents that are not, give me some documents in the middle.
So that way you have a calibration set of roughly, let's say 100 documents. And then you have a reviewer review those 100 documents. And then we're comparing your response to the response of the AI.
And the AI will say, well, if you had made changes to your prompt to, you know, add this sentence or to modify it in some way, I would have found that document responsive.

kp.d: The CTO recommends moving from calibration to a larger illustrative set of 5,000 documents only when recall and precision are satisfactory, validating again before processing a million or 10 million documents. He presents this staging as a way to reduce wasted time, expenditure and poor results. Aji is also described as supporting quality control, traditional review and privilege review, with workflows expected to evolve through customer use.
qs: you feel that you're getting good recall and good precision, then you would start to run it across, let's say, a larger set of 5,000. And then you validate it.
And then if you're comfortable with the results, you can do it on a much larger set, your million or 10 million document case.
Some folks are going to want to use it as QC.
Some people are going to want to use it for privilege review.

kp.k: Hybrid mode uses LLMs to train classical review models
kp.d: Brothers-McGrew describes a patent-pending hybrid mode in which an LLM acts as an agent to train a classical AI model using batches of 50 or 100 documents until a specified F1 score is reached. The classical model then scores the remaining case documents. He positions this as accelerating model creation while retaining an approach he says courts already trust, rather than requiring direct reliance on LLM review throughout.
qs: Also part of our patent pending technology is what we call hybrid mode.
Where we're actually using the LLM as an agent uh to train a classical AI model.
50, 100 at a time
classic AI model and use that to score all of the other documents in your case.
So using the LLM to create the model that you would build by hand today.

kp.k: Shared AI aims to reach firms of all sizes
kp.d: Jisa argues that small practices should receive the same AI access as major firms, potentially freeing time for clients or personal life. Reveal plans to maintain distinct Reveal and Logikcull platforms powered by a shared AI engine. The anticipated Aji rollout to Logikcull is Q1 2026, explicitly framed as a hope rather than a promised date; Ask early access is described as weeks away, with general availability toward year-end. These are product-access commitments and forecasts, not demonstrated reductions in unmet civil legal need.
qs: This is meant to empower everyone, not just the AmLaw 100.
We are adamant about the fact that we have two distinct e-discovery platforms that serve two distinct use cases.
the hope is that the logical customer base will have access to Aji in Q1.
Never make a promise on a date. Always give a broad 90-day window.
We want to make sure that customers, whether they're using logical or reveal, have access to the same AI technology.

kp.k: Private deployment offers a bridge rather than cloud compulsion
kp.d: Jisa says Reveal remains a cloud SaaS company but is investing profitability in Reveal Private Deployment to accommodate customers' infrastructure preferences and pace of migration. Asked about Relativity's announced requirement that new matters move to the cloud starting in 2028, he acknowledges that customer dissatisfaction with that announcement influenced Reveal's decision and created a customer-acquisition opportunity. He also acknowledges uncertain demand.

We made the decision. to invest in and make operational decisions to invest more of our profitability into RPD

I think that we heard enough people that were unhappy about the announcement that Relativity made.
that it absolutely influenced what we did.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Reveal's executives predict substantial transformation of legal work through AI, primarily through augmentation of document reviewers, and describe workflows intended to accelerate review while supporting defensibility.
pts.d: CEO Wendell Jisa predicts that legal services will be affected by AI more than any other industry and argues that collective industry action could turn law from a technology laggard into a leader. CTO Matthew Brothers-McGrew predicts that AI will let reviewers move away from document-by-document processing toward more complex problems, case understanding and client value. He explicitly presents Aji as a partner rather than a current replacement for reviewers. He describes calibration workflows that refine instructions, compare human and AI document classifications, and validate results before larger-scale deployment. He also describes a hybrid mode in which an LLM trains a classical AI model, potentially accelerating review while retaining a model type familiar to courts. These are speaker claims about intended capabilities and effects, rather than reported independent findings. Jisa argues that temporary free access will build user expertise and accelerate effective adoption when customers subsequently invest. He also promises broader access across firm sizes through Reveal and Logikcull, rather than reserving advanced AI for major firms.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on executive experience, customer conversations, historical analogy and descriptions of product design; no measured Aji performance results or specific court acceptance decisions are supplied.
pts.d: Jisa grounds his adoption outlook in his long career in legal technology and conversations with investors, executives, attorneys and investigators over the preceding 12–18 months. His argument for free access draws on his own experience becoming comfortable with ChatGPT. Brothers-McGrew uses the computer revolution as an analogy for augmentation rather than straightforward job replacement and invokes Reveal's history in AI through BrainSpace and Reveal AI. For defensibility, he points to the availability of F1, recall and precision measurements and to procedures he says are already accepted for classical AI. The transcript provides an illustrative calibration process, not a benchmark: roughly 100 human-reviewed calibration documents, followed by a larger validated batch and potentially case-wide deployment. No achieved accuracy scores, quantified savings, comparative tests, employment data or named judicial decisions are reported. The prediction that law will be affected more than any other industry is presented as Jisa's belief, without cross-industry evidence.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The executives frame transformation as already beginning in 2025, but condition wider deployment on learning, calibration, validation and customer comfort; reviewer replacement remains a speculative long-term possibility.
pts.d: Aji is announced for September 2025 on Reveal, with free access through the remainder of 2025. Jisa expresses a hope, rather than a firm commitment, for Logikcull access in Q1 of the following year. Brothers-McGrew says the current intention is augmentation; his suggestion that the market might accept reviewer replacement in 20 years is explicitly tentative. The proposed review workflow scales only after users judge recall and precision satisfactory, validate a larger sample, and become comfortable with the results. He describes continued workflow evolution over the next 10 years. Jisa qualifies his industry-leadership vision with a requirement for cooperation across companies. Both acknowledge early-stage limitations rather than claiming perfect software. The executives also support private deployment as a bridge for customers moving toward a cloud future at different speeds, although the transcript does not establish that every Aji capability will be available in every deployment environment.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The anticipated effects concern document reviewers, litigation teams, firms of all sizes and their clients, as well as legal-technology customers facing adoption and infrastructure choices.
pts.d: Brothers-McGrew identifies reviewers and litigation teams as beneficiaries of reduced repetitive processing and greater capacity for case strategy, with intended uses including quality control, traditional review and privilege review. Humans retain responsibility for reviewing calibration documents, assessing disagreements and deciding whether validated results justify scaling. Courts and opposing parties matter as audiences for evidence of defensibility, not as identified endorsers of Aji. Jisa particularly emphasizes solo and smaller firms alongside AmLaw firms and corporate customers, arguing that shared AI access can save time for clients or family life. His use of democratization concerns access to legal technology across provider sizes; the transcript does not demonstrate a reduction in unmet civil legal need. Reveal is presented as a software vendor, not as an alternative provider delivering legal work. Its free-access and private-deployment strategies are also expected to benefit Reveal commercially through later investment and customer acquisition.
